The rest of the profile centers on generic hyperarousal/dissociation and transportation-related cues, so these two triggers do not fit the trauma-specific pattern and weaken Triggers → Threat / Triggers → Memory coherence.

For this trauma type, permanent humiliation is insufficiently supported by the other selected items.

The profile’s active threat content is hyperarousal/startle and dissociative memory disturbance, and the selected strategies otherwise involve vigilance and situational avoidance. Undereating does not plausibly address any represented symptom cluster and feels disconnected from the threat/memory/appraisal pattern.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
issues.explanation: 'Avoid open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on transportation cues, startle/physical threat reactions, and trauma memory phenomena from an MVC. Open-space avoidance suggests a different threat pattern (e.g., assault/agoraphobic vulnerability) that is not represented elsewhere.

A bicycle-specific trigger is difficult to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision unless the collision specifically involved a bicycle; the rest of the profile is vehicle/crash focused rather than bicycle focused, so this item stands out as trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
issues.explanation: Alarm to unexpected touch suggests an interpersonal/assault-related threat cue more than a motor vehicle collision. In the context of the other threat items, generic startle and physical reactivity fit, but touch-specific alarm is not well linked to the reported trauma or the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is a broad social-identity appraisal that is not impossible, but it sits awkwardly with the otherwise self-blame/competence-focused appraisal pattern tied to an MVC. It is less clearly connected to the memory and trigger content than more trauma-specific appraisals would be.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Restricting food as a coping strategy is not impossible, but here it is poorly supported by the rest of the profile. The formulation strongly links threat and appraisals to maladaptive strategies, and the other strategies are vehicle avoidance and thought monitoring, whereas undereating addresses a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

vignette:
James

James was sixty-seven when the pickup truck ran the red light and T-boned his sedan on a Tuesday afternoon in November. He had been driving home from the VA clinic where he worked as a civilian medic three days a week, a job that had kept him anchored since his wife, Patricia, died five years earlier. The impact came from his left. He remembered the sound first-a compression of metal and glass, a noise so complete it seemed to erase everything else. The truck driver had been drinking; James smelled it immediately when the man stumbled out of his cab, a sharp reek of whiskey and beer that cut through the smell of burning rubber and hot engine oil. James, who had spent forty years as a combat medic in the Army, who had stabilized men with catastrophic wounds on three continents, found himself unable to move. His left leg was trapped. When the paramedics arrived, they had to use the Jaws of Life.

The physical injuries healed within months. The fracture in his tibia mended. The lacerations closed. But something had fractured in James that no X-ray could show. By the time he was cleared to return to work, he had stopped driving. At first it was just a caution-his left leg still ached, and the thought of gripping a steering wheel made his chest tight. But as weeks passed, the caution hardened into something else. He could not sit in the passenger seat without his hands beginning to shake. The moment a car approached an intersection, his body would tense. He had come to believe that he could not be trusted behind the wheel, that some failure of judgment or reflex on his part had caused the collision, though the police report clearly stated he had the green light. The thought made no logical sense to him, yet it persisted with the weight of absolute truth. He was a weak person-not physically, but in some deeper way. A strong person would have seen it coming. A strong person would have reacted differently.

He began taking the bus to the VA clinic, a forty-minute journey each way. His supervisor, Dr. Reeves, asked him once if everything was all right. James said yes, but the question lodged in his mind. He watched his own thoughts constantly now, monitoring them for signs that he was losing coherence, that the trauma was fracturing his mind the way it had fractured his body. Whenever he caught himself thinking about the crash, he would forcibly redirect his attention-to a patient's chart, to the weather, to anything else. This worked for short stretches, but the thoughts always returned, often accompanied by the sound of the impact, a deep metallic crunch that played in his head as if a speaker were embedded in his skull.

The worst part was that he could not explain any of this to anyone. When Dr. Reeves asked again, more directly, James opened his mouth to describe what had happened and found that the narrative fragmented. He could see the truck approaching, could smell the alcohol, but when he tried to string these moments into a coherent account, the thread snapped. The memory felt borrowed, as though he were recounting something that had happened to another man, not to himself. This terrified him more than the physical panic did. The fear that he was losing his grip on reality.

At home in the evenings, James would startle at ordinary sounds-the refrigerator humming, a car door closing on the street outside, the neighbor's dog barking. His body would jolt, his heart would race, and it would take minutes for him to settle. He had stopped going to the grocery store because the smell of burnt meat at the deli counter triggered a cascade of physical reactions that left him shaking in the parking lot. The smell of alcohol-anywhere, anytime-sent a spike of adrenaline through his chest.

It was his daughter, calling from Portland, who finally said the words he needed to hear: that he should talk to someone. That what he was experiencing was not weakness, not insanity, but something that could be addressed. At sixty-seven, James had survived wars, had held dying men's hands, had built a life after loss. Yet he could not cross the threshold of his own front door without fear. He called the VA and asked for a referral to mental health. He was terrified of what the answer might be, but he was more terrified of continuing as he was-trapped in a car that no longer moved, a man who could not trust himself, a medic who could no longer heal.
